schema.title: Credentials
schema.description:
A set of credentials: a login for SFTP, FTPS, the web portal and the S3-compatible endpoint. The API calls this resource `users`.

Each set of credentials has its own password, file access and network rules, so you can give each
system its own and revoke one without affecting the others.

File access takes one of two forms. With a **home directory**, `Permission` applies everywhere
from `ChrootDirectory` down. With **virtual folders** (`HomeDirectoryDetails`), the credentials
see only the listed folders, each with its own permission, and `Permission` is absent.

Credentials created before a field existed may not have it, so treat fields that aren't required
as optional.

Id.description: Unique identifier, used in the URL of every request about these credentials. It's also the login name when you don't set `UserName`.

OrganizationId.description: The organization these credentials belong to.

UserName.description: The login name. Unique across SFTP To Go, not just your organization.

Alias.description: A label shown in the dashboard. Defaults to `UserName`; an empty string resets it to `UserName`.

State.description: Whether the credentials can connect. Credentials also become `inactive` when they expire.

Permission.description:
What the credentials can do with files under their chroot directory. Absent when they use virtual folders.

- `none`: can connect, but sees nothing. The default.
- `read-only`: download and list.
- `write-only`: upload only; folders can be listed, files can't be read.
- `read-write-no-delete`: download and upload, including replacing a file, but never delete or rename.
- `read-write`: download, upload and delete.
- `full`: read-write, plus sharing files from the web portal.

Host.description: The hostname the credentials connect to. Uses your custom domain if you have one.

HomeDirectory.description: The directory the credentials land in after connecting. Defaults to `/home/{UserName}`.

ChrootDirectory.description: The highest directory the credentials can reach. Defaults to `/`. Ignored when they use virtual folders.

HomeDirectoryDetails.description: Virtual folders: the folders the credentials see, each mapped to a location in your storage with its own permission. Absent when they use a home directory.

items.title: VirtualFolder
items.description: One virtual folder: a path the credentials see, mapped to a location in your storage, with its own permission.

Entry.description: The path the credentials see, such as `/inbound`. Must start with a slash and not end with one. The root `/` must be the only entry. Entries can't share a path, contain one another, or contain a variable such as `${...}`.

Target.description: The location in your storage, as a path from the root of your bucket. Must start with a slash and not end with one. Two entries can show the same location only with the same permission.

Type.description: Whether the entry is a folder or a single file. Defaults to `DIRECTORY`. A `FILE` entry can't be the root `/`.

Permission.description: What the credentials can do inside this entry, with the same levels as `Permission` on the credentials. `none` keeps the entry listed but denies everything in it.

SupportedProtocols.description:
How the credentials can sign in: normally `SFTP`, `FTPS` and `WEB_PORTAL`.

If their virtual folders are too many or too deep for SFTP and FTPS, this lists only
`WEB_PORTAL`; shorten or remove folders to restore the others. Absent on older credentials,
which can use all three.

items.description: A way the credentials can sign in.

Email.description: Where web portal invitations and password resets are sent. Not needed for credentials used only by a machine.

EmailVerified.description: Whether the email address is confirmed. Set when the recipient follows the verification link; you can't set it directly.

IsDefault.description: Whether these are the organization's default credentials. Default credentials can't be deleted and always use a home directory.

SshPublicKeysCount.description: How many SSH public keys are attached.

SshPublicKeys.description: The attached SSH public keys. Returned only when you retrieve one set of credentials.

items.title: SshPublicKey
items.description: A public key attached to a set of credentials, for key-based SFTP sign-in.

UserId.description: The `Id` of the credentials the key is attached to.

OrganizationId.description: The organization the key belongs to.

SshPublicKeyBody.description: The public key, in OpenSSH format.

Curve.description: The elliptic curve, for `ecdsa` and `ed25519` keys.

Comment.description: The comment at the end of the key, often the owner's name or machine.

Fingerprint.description: The key's SHA-256 fingerprint, as `ssh-keygen -l` shows it.

CreatedAt.description: When the key was attached, in Unix epoch milliseconds.

UpdatedAt.description: When the key last changed, in Unix epoch milliseconds.

Settings.title: CredentialsSettings
Settings.description: Security and network settings for one set of credentials.

Security.description: How the person using these credentials proves who they are in the web portal.

MFA.description: Multi-factor authentication for web portal sign-in. It doesn't apply to SFTP, FTPS or S3 connections.

Required.description: Whether the person must enrol and use a second factor to sign in to the portal.

Factors.description: The second factors enrolled for these credentials. Empty until one is added.

items.title: MfaFactor
items.description: A second factor enrolled for web portal sign-in. The person using the credentials enrolls it in the portal; this API can't.

Type.description: The kind of factor: `totp` for an authenticator app, or `email` for a code sent to the credentials' email address.

Description.description: A label the person gave the factor when enrolling it.

CodeLength.description: How many digits the one-time codes for this factor have.

IsPrimary.description: Whether this factor is offered first at sign-in.

Protocols.description: Where the factor is asked for. Always the web portal.

items.description: A protocol the factor applies to.

LastAuthAt.description: When the factor was last used to sign in, in Unix epoch milliseconds, or `null`.

CreatedAt.description: When the factor was enrolled, in Unix epoch milliseconds.

UpdatedAt.description: When the factor last changed, in Unix epoch milliseconds.

Network.description: Where these credentials may connect from, in addition to your organization's own rules.

InboundRules.description: Rules that allow connections to these credentials, in addition to your organization's rules. Empty by default.

items.title: InboundRule
items.description:
A network rule that allows connections to a set of credentials from an address or range.

A connection is allowed when any enabled `allow` rule matches its protocol and source address,
counting your organization's rules and the credentials' rules together. Rules on credentials can
only add to what the organization allows. New organizations start with one organization rule that
allows every address; tighten it before rules on credentials make a difference.

Id.description: An identifier you choose, unique within these credentials. The dashboard uses a UUID.

Protocol.description: The connections the rule applies to: `*` for every protocol, or `SFTP`, `FTPS` or `WEB_PORTAL`. Case-sensitive.

State.description: Whether the rule is in effect. A `disabled` rule is kept but never matches.

Action.description: What a matching connection may do. Only `allow` rules are evaluated.

Source.description: An IPv4 or IPv6 address, or a CIDR range such as `203.0.113.0/24`.

Description.description: A note explaining why the rule exists. Shown in the dashboard.

ExpiresAt.description:
When access stops, in **Unix epoch seconds**. `null` or absent means the credentials don't expire.

Once the time passes (checked every few minutes), the credentials become `inactive` and
`ExpiresAt` returns to `null`. Activating them restores access with no expiry.

LastLogin.description: The most recent sign-in, or `null` if the credentials have never been used. Not returned when credentials are created.

oneOf.title: LastLogin
oneOf.description: The most recent time these credentials connected, and from where.

Id.description: The identifier of the audit log event that recorded the login.

Timestamp.description: When the login happened, in Unix epoch milliseconds.

IpAddress.description: The anonymized source address. An IPv4 address keeps its first three parts and an IPv6 address its first 48 bits; the rest is zeroed.

OriginalIpAddress.description: The full address the connection came from.

Geo.description: The approximate location of the address, or `null` if it couldn't be located. A connection through a VPN or proxy shows the proxy's location.

oneOf.description: The approximate location of the address.
The address could not be located.

UserAgent.description: The client as it identified itself, parsed into application, operating system and device, or `null` if it sent nothing. Unrecognized parts are `Other` or `null`.

userAgent.description: The raw identification string the client sent.

patchMinor.description: The version part after the patch, when there is one.

oneOf.description: The client did not identify itself.
The credentials have never been used.

LoginsCount.description: How many times the credentials have signed in. Not returned when they are created.

Password.description:
The current password, in clear text.

It's returned on every read, so treat any response that contains credentials as a secret:
don't log it, cache it or send it to a browser you don't control.

PasswordCreatedAt.description: When the password was set, as an ISO 8601 timestamp. Not returned when credentials are created.

URI.description: A connection string with the login name, password and host. It contains the password in clear text.

CreatedAt.description: When the credentials were created, in Unix epoch milliseconds.

UpdatedAt.description: When the credentials were last changed, in Unix epoch milliseconds.

400.description:
The request body is invalid. Nothing was changed.

`errors` lists the rejected fields and why, either as an object keyed by field name or as a list
of fields; handle both. Fix the request rather than retrying it.

schema.title: Error
schema.description: Every error response has this shape. Match on `id`, which is stable, not on `message`, which may change.

id.description:
A stable, machine-readable code for the error, such as `invalid_request_body`, `not_found`
or `internal_server_error`.

message.description: A human-readable explanation, safe to log but not intended for end users verbatim.

errors.description: The fields that were rejected, and why. Present only on `400` responses, either as an object keyed by field name or as a list of fields. Handle both.

oneOf.title: ValidationError
oneOf.description:
Field-level detail on a `400` caused by an invalid request body.

Each validated field appears as its own property, keyed by its name as sent; nested fields use
dotted paths such as `Settings.Network`. Fields that passed are listed too, with `isInvalid:
false`, so filter on `isInvalid` to find the failures.

isValid.description: Always `false` when this object is returned.

additionalProperties.description: The outcome for one field of the request body.

message.description: Why the field was rejected. Empty when the field passed.

HasActions.message: You must include at least one action.

items.title: FieldError
items.description: One field that was rejected, and why.

field.description: The name of the field, as it was sent.

message.description: Why the field was rejected, written for a person.
examples: Unfortunately, two virtual folders can't share the same path.

fields.summary: A field failed the checks every request goes through

401.description:
The request isn't authenticated.

The `Authorization` header is missing or malformed, the key is revoked, the key belongs to another
organization than the one in the path, or the organization isn't active.

The body takes two shapes: a bare `message` when the request is rejected before it reaches the
endpoint, or the standard error with `id` when the endpoint rejects it. Handle both.

schema.title: UnauthorizedError
schema.description:
The body of a `401`.

When authentication fails, the request is rejected before it reaches the endpoint and the body has
only `message`. When an endpoint rejects an authenticated request, the body is the standard error,
with `id`. So `id` is optional on this status only.

id.description:
A stable, machine-readable code. Absent when the request was rejected before reaching the
endpoint.

message.description: A human-readable explanation of why the request was not authenticated.

403.description: Your plan's limit on credentials is reached, or your organization is still being set up. The `message` says which. Delete credentials you no longer need or upgrade, or retry in a few minutes.

500.description:
Something failed on our side.

A change may or may not have been made, so retrieve the credentials before you retry one. Retrying
a read is always safe. If the error persists, contact support with the time of the request.
